name: Oxytocin nasal spray

lead: Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid hormone involved in childbirth, milk ejection and social bonding. In looksmaxxing and peptide communities the nasal spray is used for sociability, mood and a more relaxed, confident presence, and some threads extend this to bone and facial-structure claims.

Given into the nose, it is thought to reach brain circuits involved in social cognition. Lab studies report reduced amygdala responses to fearful faces and altered behaviour in trust games, with results varying by person and context. No published trial has tested it for facial appearance or attractiveness.

paras: People use it as a nasal spray before social situations or as part of a mood routine, often bought from online vendors as peptide kits. Effects in studies are short-term, so use is typically situational.

Systemic oxytocin in obstetrics is a high-alert medication, with risks such as uterine hyperstimulation and water intoxication at excessive doses. Short-term research use by nose has not produced serious adverse events in published studies, but long-term data are limited. It is a prescription drug in the US and UK, and gray-market sprays are not regulated for purity or concentration.

social.title: Study: "Cuddle hormone" oxytocin nasal spray helps against loneliness

angle.text: Oxytocin nasal spray is used for a calmer, more confident social presence by acting on social-bonding circuits in the brain. Lab studies have examined it for trust and anxiety; no study supports it for facial structure or attractiveness.

lead: Intranasal oxytocin is the hormone oxytocin delivered as a nasal spray so that it can reach the brain. Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid peptide made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary; it drives uterine contraction in labor and milk ejection, and acts on brain circuits involved in bonding and social behaviour.[1][2][3] A synthetic form is a standard obstetric drug given by infusion or injection, and the nasal route is the one researchers use to test the hormone's behavioural effects.[3]

The appearance angle is indirect and mostly claimed: people in peptide and looksmaxxing circles discuss the spray for sociability, ease in social situations, bonding and mood, which they treat as part of presenting oneself well, rather than for any change to the face or body. Online vendors sell or discuss peptide spray kits for these purposes.[4]

Research on intranasal oxytocin is large and contested. The best-known study, a 2005 Nature experiment, reported that people who received the spray showed more trust in a monetary game; later reviews found that the effects of oxytocin in humans depend on context and on the person, and a 2022 review in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B concluded that the evidence for oxytocin as a 'social neuropeptide' is weak if the most highly cited papers represent the best evidence.[5][6][7] No published human trial has examined intranasal oxytocin for facial appearance, bone structure or attractiveness.[3]

paras: Oxytocin is a cyclic nonapeptide encoded by the OXT gene and made in magnocellular neurons of the hypothalamus. It is released into the blood from the posterior pituitary and also acts as a neurotransmitter within the brain.[1][8] Its receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor present in uterine muscle, the mammary gland and brain regions linked to social behaviour.[1]

Intranasal delivery is used in research because oxytocin in the bloodstream has a very short half-life, about three minutes after intravenous dosing, and enters the brain poorly; intranasal use is associated with a central duration of roughly two and a quarter to four hours.[3] Wikipedia's oxytocin article reports that single intranasal doses raised blood oxytocin about two- to three-fold for only an hour or so, that cerebrospinal fluid levels did not rise until about 75 minutes after administration, and that circulating levels did not correlate with cerebrospinal fluid levels.[9] How much of an intranasal dose reaches the brain directly versus acting through the periphery remains debated.[3][9]

In obstetrics, oxytocin is given by infusion or injection to induce or strengthen labor and to reduce bleeding after delivery, and it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[3] It was added to the Institute for Safe Medication Practices high-alert list in 2012 because of the harm that can follow dosing errors.[3]

The intranasal form is not approved in the US for social anxiety, autism or other behavioural conditions, although they have been research targets.[8] Wikipedia's medication article says an intranasal spray is also used as a supplement for psychiatric, endocrine and weight-management purposes.[3]

For looksmaxxing readers the relevant claims are about presentation rather than anatomy: feeling calmer and warmer in social situations, reading faces better and bonding. Research frames these as effects on trust, recognition of social and fear cues and memory for social information such as faces.[3][10] Forum threads discuss spray kits aimed at these goals, sometimes combined with other peptides.

Henry Dale described the uterus-contracting action of pituitary extract in 1906. Ott and Scott (1910) and Schafer and Mackenzie (1911) described its milk-ejection property, and William Blair-Bell made the first clinical use of oxytocin in 1909 to induce labor in complicated births.[9][8] Vincent du Vigneaud determined its structure in 1952 and synthesised it in 1953, the first polypeptide hormone to be sequenced and synthesised, and received the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.[9][3]

Research on its social effects expanded in the 2000s, notably after the 2005 trust experiment and work on social stress buffering, in which social support and oxytocin together suppressed cortisol and subjective stress responses.[5][11] Neuroeconomist Paul Zak, co-author of the 2005 Nature study, popularised the hormone as the 'moral molecule' in a 2012 book and a 2011 TED talk; the book linked oxytocin to empathy, altruism and morality.[12]

In the 2005 Nature study, participants given intranasal oxytocin showed more trust toward another person in a monetary investment game than those given placebo. Wikipedia reports that nasal oxytocin recipients showed the highest level of trust about twice as often as controls, that the effect did not appear when subjects believed they were playing a computer, and that the authors took this to mean oxytocin does not just reduce risk aversion.[5][9] Other studies reported that recipients rated neutral faces as more trustworthy, that generosity rose in the Ultimatum Game but not the Dictator Game, and that empathy in healthy men increased, which has been linked to enhanced eye gaze.[9]

A neuroimaging study reported that intranasal oxytocin reduced amygdala activation to fearful faces and weakened its coupling with brainstem regions, giving a proposed mechanism for reduced fear and social anxiety.[10] A 2021 randomized study reported that oxytocin facilitates socially directed attention.[13]

A 2011 review argued that the social effects of oxytocin in humans depend on context and individual differences.[6] Critics have noted that oxytocin can also increase envy, gloating and in-group bias; Zak's critics argue that raising the salience of social cues may explain results and that his trust studies raise methodological questions, while Zak responds that endogenous oxytocin release eliminates in-group bias.[12] Wikipedia's article states that serious methodological questions have arisen about the role of oxytocin in trust and generosity, and that publication bias and selective outcome reporting may affect reproducibility.[9]

The 2022 Royal Society B review mapped the literature into clusters (animal mechanistic studies, observational studies, intranasal intervention studies and translational patient studies), analysed the most highly cited papers in each and concluded that the evidence for the 'social neuropeptide' claim is weak if those represent the best evidence.[7] A 2011 review described oxytocin and vasopressin as social neuropeptides of interest for translational medicine,[14] and a broader review of human oxytocin research, by contrast, described the findings in healthy subjects as encouraging while identifying urgent needs for information on optimal dosing strategies and interactions with other systems.[15]
No studies found on intranasal oxytocin for appearance, facial structure or attractiveness. Studies of intranasal oxytocin for other purposes include the following.

A 24-week randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial of intranasal oxytocin in children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 with autism spectrum disorder was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021.[16] Wikipedia notes a 2013 meta-analysis in which only autism spectrum disorder showed a significant pooled effect, and a 2022 study that found an effect in children aged 3 to 5 but not 5 to 12.[3] Grokipedia states that NIH-funded trials found no significant improvement in social functioning in autism and that, in social anxiety, intranasal oxytocin did not enhance the outcome of exposure therapy.[8] A review of oxytocin in anxiety disorders covers receptor-gene variation, attachment style and social anxiety severity.[17]

Other registered or published work includes a phase 2 study of intranasal oxytocin in hypothalamic obesity (18 participants, completed),[18] a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intranasal oxytocin in adults with obesity,[19] a phase 2 trial in frontotemporal dementia (112 participants, status unknown),[20] and a phase 2 study of peripheral oxytocin and touch in healthy adults (20 participants, completed).[21] Wikipedia lists other proposed uses such as PTSD and relationship counseling, describing evidence as limited.[3]

Wikipedia reports that short-term intranasal doses used in research have not been associated with recorded serious adverse effects, whereas systemic oxytocin in obstetrics can cause uterine hyperstimulation, and prolonged or excessive dosing is linked to water intoxication, seizures and uterine rupture; arrhythmias and anaphylaxis have also been reported.[3] The article states there is no robust evidence that oxytocin causes autism or other neurodevelopmental disorders.[3] The 2014 pediatric review notes that more must be learned about the risks of repeated use on the developing brain and body.[22]

Long-term safety of repeated self-directed intranasal use has not been studied in controlled trials. Compounded or gray-market products have no consistent quality oversight, and counterfeit oxytocin products have been reported in some countries.[3]

Oxytocin is prescription-only in the US and UK.[3] Online vendors market oxytocin and other peptides as nasal sprays for sociability and bonding; a looksmax.org thread discusses a UK peptide spray kit with a dilution check for N-acetyl semax alongside oxytocin. No standards govern concentration or purity of such gray-market kits.[3]

Other threads discuss testing oxytocin together with growth hormone and parathyroid hormone analogs, and experimenting with oxytocin spray in connection with the 'ndpill', a community term for a belief about nondating outcomes.[4] Separately, some users talk about oxytocin as a feeling to be reduced after romantic attachment; one thread asks how to 'nuke' oxytocin after meeting a woman, and a reply says the hormone is useful for bone growth while another proposes seeking rejection to end the feeling. These are individual forum opinions, not research findings.

lore.intro: Oxytocin spray appears in looksmaxxing forums mostly in peptide-kit threads and in discussions of bonding and attachment rather than as a facial-improvement tool.

claims.claim: Oxytocin spray can fix social anxiety or the "ndpill" mindset.
Oxytocin from sex or relationships can be "nuked" or avoided by following specific routines.
Oxytocin supports bone growth, so it is relevant to facial structure.
Peptide spray kits combining oxytocin with other compounds are a convenient way to use these peptides.
Oxytocin is the 'trust' or 'moral' molecule that makes people more trusting.
Nasal oxytocin reduces fear and social anxiety by calming the amygdala.
The spray gets oxytocin into the brain.
